steps: Viruses are not placed in any of the three domains: Bacteria, Archaea or Eukarya.
They are acellular and lack the structures of a cell, such as cytoplasm and ribosomes.
They do not carry out metabolism independently and can reproduce only inside a living host cell.
The three-domain classification is based on differences among cellular organisms, so it does not readily classify viruses.
items.finalAnswer: Viruses are acellular and depend on host cells to reproduce, so they do not fit within the three domains of cellular life.

steps: Each organism is given a two-word scientific name: the first word is the genus and the second is the species name.
Scientific names are Latin or are latinised, so they can be used internationally.
The genus name begins with a capital letter; the species name begins with a lowercase letter.
In print, both words are written in italics; when handwritten, each word is underlined separately.
A scientific name should be unique and follow the accepted rules of biological nomenclature.
An example is *Homo sapiens*.
items.finalAnswer: A scientific name has two Latin or latinised words: a capitalised genus followed by a lowercase species name; it is italicised in print or underlined separately when handwritten.

steps: An organism placed in the wrong group may be mistaken for a different organism or its relationships to other organisms may be misunderstood.
Its conservation status and protection needs may be assessed incorrectly, causing conservation efforts or resources to be misdirected.
Scientific studies based on the incorrect identification may produce unreliable results about its distribution, ecology or evolution.
Correct classification helps scientists identify organisms accurately and make informed conservation decisions.
items.finalAnswer: Incorrect classification can misdirect conservation efforts and make scientific findings about an organism unreliable.

steps: Observe and record the organism's characteristics, such as its structure and other distinguishing features.
Compare these characteristics with those of known organisms, using identification keys and scientific references.
Place the organism in the appropriate taxonomic groups, from kingdom through to genus and species, based on its similarities and differences.
Check whether it is already known; if it is a new species, prepare a clear description that distinguishes it from related species.
Choose a two-word Latin or latinised name: a capitalised genus name followed by a lowercase species name.
Write the name in italics in print, or underline each word separately when handwritten, and publish the description and name according to the accepted rules of nomenclature.
items.finalAnswer: Compare and identify the organism, assign its taxonomic groups, then describe and publish it with a unique two-word name following the rules of binomial nomenclature.
